How do you interpret your "an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution"? How much does the source of this new mathematical argument/proof step matter, its publishing outlets etc. And should this qualify even if there was more than one independent solution to any of the open problems (there might be—if the correct solution is very complex but not obvious, this might well happen).
* For each of the dates, list the qualitative category (P>99%, P>95%, P>80%, ... etc.) and, if necessary, specify each of those probabilities. Then list any new probability categories (P<20%, 10%, 1%, 0.1%, 0.01%, etc.) into which the event has shifted and preferably with a numbers (say P<0.001%) in which it is essentially impossible to happen (note that if this shift has happened, this currently nonexistent part of the forecast _must move sideways to P=99.999%\)
* Use the probabilities of (1) for these probabilities.
* Also list the (1) probabilities of the qualitatively opposite status (another evidence for the opposite side that has more or changing odds than the opposing side currently happens, thus leaves the event more likely than not to happen one day from now)

Data stolen from "AI foresight- color coding" table.

Note that in this mode, "nothing to say" should also be stated. "Qualitatively impossible" for all probabilities represents the event can't happen at all, because all reasons for it to happen are qualitative reasons, not expressions of reasoning with force, countering obvious or common reasons against its happening, ie reasons that by themselves, or supported by evidence reasoning, prove offline that the event will not happen, or that its chance of happening will not grow from zero to 1-a-trillionth: 

(*a.) Useful evidence >95% chance heuristic: "at least 2 reasons supporting one side, and one cited one against one side, or 3 reasons each as above, could work in favor of either of the two heuristics, if the two heuristics have equal 95% probability)

Note that most evidence from (a.) is prejudiced, and merely amounts to suggesting one side slightly rather than very likely given that heuristic: if in (a.) the undeniably true-pole estimates need to be disproportionately large for the blue-cell heuristic, this shows racing humanity due to the dominance of theory offers a slightly-more-favorable model. If it's the red-cell heuristic, this suggests the opposite, a slightly-favorable view of the red cell (which may be random swings in red or blue pole estimates).

Before forecasters have given their speculations about one side clearly being more appropriate, if you can make the two the same probability heuristic-quantity, then you can change the overall evidence-probability itself—so that subtle bias toward the opposing side, suppression of much-quantitatively-undeniable evidence that fits, etc. has happened—for example, "only 50% chance x may happen," when 50% can make a large difference given the massive quantitative differences between 0.1% and 99.1% vs. 0.2% and 99.8%.

Finally, Qualitative impossible: No reason (a) to happen, only one reason in favor (mostly unseen) vs. a reason "that won't exist by the time of the forecast" for it to not happen now, and ~25-40% undeniably true reasons why it self-corrects by `time_limit`.

Forecast qualitatively impossible: "the event can't happen at all, because all reasons for it to happen are qualitative reasons, not expressions of reasoning of force countering obvious or common reasons against its happening, ie reasons proved offline that the event won't happen, or the chance of it happening having not grown from 0 to 1-a-trillionth"

For the "it can't happen" heuristic, one can find charts showing that a significant reduction of AI risk is correlated with decrease of chances the neutral CGP will occur.
formatted_prompt:
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.
